title: Self-Evolving Deep Research via Joint Generation and Evaluation

paper.title: Self-Evolving Deep Research via Joint Generation and Evaluation
paper.abstract: Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) have become increasingly adopted in daily applications, with deep research standing out as a particularly important capability. Unlike traditional question-answering (QA) tasks, deep research report generation lacks definitive ground-truth, making reward design inherently unverifiable and limiting effective reinforcement learning. Existing approaches mitigate this challenge with LLM-as-a-judge and query-dependent evaluation rubrics, but they still rely on static evaluators that cannot adapt their standards as the solver improves, leading to insufficient and eventually saturated optimization pressure. We address this limitation with a s elf-evolving co -evolutionary training framework for deep re search evaluation and generation ( SCORE ), which tightly couples an evaluator and a solver in a shared-parameter learning process. Rather than treating generation and evaluation as isolated modules, we leverage their intrinsic connection to enable joint improvement within a single shared-parameter model. To restrict this process, we introduce a meta-harness, which dynamically controls the evaluation environment based on solver performance, encouraging valid evaluation dimensions and sufficiently deep evaluator search. Extensive experiments on deep research benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvement in report generation quality, showing that co-evolving evaluation and generation is a promising direction for training open-ended research agents.

Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Chengkun Cai Yuanfeng Song Xing Chen Affiliation: University College London Sirui Han Yike Guo Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Affiliation: ByteDance, China Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) have become increasingly adopted in daily applications, with deep research standing out as a particularly important capability. Unlike traditional question-answering (QA) tasks, deep research report generation lacks definitive ground-truth, making reward design inherently unverifiable and limiting effective reinforcement learning. Existing approaches mitigate this challenge with LLM-as-a-judge and query-dependent evaluation rubrics, but they still rely on static evaluators that cannot adapt their standards as the solver improves, leading to insufficient and eventually saturated optimization pressure. We address this limitation with a s elf-evolving co -evolutionary training framework for deep re search evaluation and generation ( SCORE ), which tightly couples an evaluator and a solver in a shared-parameter learning process. Rather than treating generation and evaluation as isolated modules, we leverage their intrinsic connection to enable joint improvement within a single shared-parameter model. To restrict this process, we introduce a meta-harness, which dynamically controls the evaluation environment based on solver performance, encouraging valid evaluation dimensions and sufficiently deep evaluator search. Extensive experiments on deep research benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvement in report generation quality, showing that co-evolving evaluation and generation is a promising direction for training open-ended research agents. 1 Introduction Figure 1 : Empirical evidence of the positive correlation between LLMs’ generation and evaluation capabilities. Owing to their extraordinary capabilities, Large Language Models (LLMs) have become deeply integrated into various complex domains, spanning autonomous driving [ 48 ] , software development [ 9 ] , multimedia generation [ 33 , 46 , 54 ] and so on [ 49 , 25 ] . As the demand for comprehensive information retrieval and synthesis grows, enhancing the deep research capabilities of LLMs has attracted increasing attention from researchers. Several search agents, such as GPT-Researcher [ 13 ] and AgentCPM-Explore [ 2 ] , have recently demonstrated remarkable proficiency in these multi-hop research tasks. Furthermore, previous works like Search-o1 [ 26 ] and SSP [ 30 ] have shown that applying Reinforcement Learning (RL) to these models can substantially enhance their reasoning capabilities when integrated into agent, yielding significant performance improvements on complex Question-Answering (QA) tasks. Differ from traditional QA tasks, training models for open-ended report generation presents two challenges. First, comprehensive reports lack a definitive ground truth, making objective reward signals inherently difficult to define [ 23 , 12 ] . Since there is no absolute standard for open-ended queries, relying on human annotations for generated reports is prohibitively expensive, making objective and scalable reward signals difficult to construct. Relying on human annotations to cover these diverse paths is prohibitively expensive and difficult to scale. Second, the evaluation criteria for a high-quality report are multi-dimensional and query-related [ 21 , 10 ] . Single fixed evaluation metric inevitably ignore crucial dimensions including factual correctness and insight diversity for different questions. This dimensional omission results in sparse training signals and fails to provide the fine-grained credit assignment required for complex generation tasks. To overcome these challenges in report generation, recent research proposes several novel paradigms to provide more effective optimization signals. WebThinker [ 27 ] and Step-DeepResearch [ 16 ] have applied the LLM-as-a-judge [ 57 ] to evaluate report quality during the training process. AdaRubric [ 8 ] proposes a framework that dynamically generates task-specific evaluation criteria based on the input instructions. Mix-GRM [ 52 ] utilizes Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to automatically adapt between breadth-first (B-CoT) and depth-first (D-CoT) evaluation strategies according to distinct task demands. However, a fixed external evaluator lacks the ability to dynamically adjust its evaluation standards, and therefore fails to provide sustained optimization pressure as the solver improves. As empirically observed in Figure 1 , LLMs’ generation quality is positively correlated with its evaluation proficiency. Building upon this insight, we hypothesize that generation and evaluation abilities can be mutually reinforcing and should be optimized within a unified, rather than decoupled, architecture. To this end, we propose a self-play framework in which the policy model iteratively generates and evaluate reports. By replacing a fixed external judge with a dynamic evaluator that evolves alongside the solver, our method maintains informative training pressure throughout learning. Furthermore, a Meta-Harness [ 22 ] is applied to stabilize this process by enforcing environmental constraints. Empirically, this co-evolutionary paradigm brings substantial and consistent improvements across diverse research generation tasks. In a nutshell, our contributions are summarized as below: • We propose SCORE, an evaluator-solver self-play framework for training deep research agents with unverifiable rewards. This framework provide dynamic, multidimensional rewards to optimize the solver’s ability in open-ended report generation, constrained by a meta-harness. • We provide a theoretical analysis of SCORE under shared parameters. Our analysis clarifies the role of consistency in evaluator-side adaptation and characterizes the local optimization behavior of shared-parameter alternating updates. • We show that our method improves agent performance across multiple evaluation dimensions on deep research benchmarks, and provide a systematic analysis of how parameters affect training procedure under unverifiable rewards. 2 Related Work 2.1 Deep Research LLMs have exhibited strong deep research capabilities in recent agent studies [ 59 , 1 ] . Initial frameworks, including Search-o1 [ 26 ] , Search-R1 [ 20 ] , and R1-Searcher [ 39 ] , successfully introduced explicit reasoning process into agentic search frameworks, yielding substantial empirical improvement in multi-hop question-answering (QA) tasks. Following these advancements, researchers integrated diverse optimization algorithms into agentic training pipelines. Specifically, WebThinker [ 27 ] utilizes iterative Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) for deep research agents, whereas DeepResearcher [ 58 ] adopts Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Diverging from these algorithmic enhancements, SimpleDeepSearcher [ 40 ] argues that the quality of the training data supersedes the specific training paradigm. Beyond QA tasks, report generation tasks are inherently more complex, as they involve open-ended, multi-faceted synthesis where establishing reliable ground truth for automated evaluation remains a critical bottleneck. To address this complexity, multi-agent frameworks like STORM and Co-STORM leverage preliminary knowledge and human-in-the-loop interactions during report generation [ 34 , 19 ] . Later approaches such as Step-DeepResearch and AgentCPM-Report [ 16 , 28 ] directly integrate model training optimized for their specific agent frameworks. 2.2 Intrinsic Rewards and Self-Play Traditional Self-play is widely applied to agentic studies as an adversarial reinforcement learning approach [ 53 ] . AbsoluteZero, R-Zero, SeRL and SPIRAL, demonstrate the effectiveness of self-evolution in tackling complex reasoning tasks under data scarcity situation [ 55 , 17 , 29 , 11 ] . Recent frameworks, including Search Self-play, Dr. Zero, and SPaR, demonstrate the substantial advantages of applying this technique to search agents operating within multi-hop environments [ 30 , 50 , 3 ] . Beyond adversarial learning paradigms like proposer-solver self-play, alternative approaches propose training solvers on filtered trajectories generated by the models themselves, as demonstrated by frameworks such as WebThinker, EvolveSearch, and EXSEARCH [ 27 , 51 , 38 ] . Other notable efforts include AceSearcher, which employs cooperative interaction between decomposer and solver for self-improvement [ 45 ] . Moreover, optimization strategies utilizing internal rewards provided by models themselves have been adopted by researchers in frameworks such as INTUITOR [ 56 ] and JEPO [ 41 ] . These previous works demonstrate the efficacy of internal signals in enhancing autonomous capability improvements. However, the unique characteristics fo deep research task present a significant evaluation challenge. The difficulty of reliably scoring open-domain, comprehensive reports makes it highly challenging to design effective reward signals that resolve the credit assignment issue. 3 Methodology Figure 2 : SCORE is controlled by Meta-Harness. The evaluator first selects evaluation dimensions from a provided dimension pool and retrieves evidence accordingly. The solver is updated using rewards derived from evaluator, while the evaluator is optimized based on the consistency of rollout reports generated by the solver. A reward verifier filters out invalid rewards before they are used for solver optimization. 3.1 Problem Setting We study deep research report generation , where the goal is to learn a policy π ⁡ ( r ∣ q , ℰ q ) \pi(r\mid q,\mathcal{E}_{q}) over candidate reports r r for a given query q q and environment ℰ q \mathcal{E}_{q} . We assume that report quality is governed by a latent functional Q ⁡ ( r , q , ℰ q ) , Q(r;q,\mathcal{E}_{q}), and the ideal objective is to assign more probability mass to reports with higher latent quality. Here, q ∈ 𝒬 q\in\mathcal{Q} denotes a user query, r ∈ ℛ r\in\mathcal{R} denotes a candidate long-form report, and ℰ q \mathcal{E}_{q} denotes the query-specific evidence and evaluation environment. Unlike QA-style tasks, Q Q is inherently multi-dimensional and query-dependent : a report may succeed or fail along different axes, such as factual support, evidence coverage, citation grounding, contradiction handling, uncertainty calibration, and discourse coherence. As a result, long-form report generation rarely admits a single reliable verifier or a fixed scalar reward that is both sufficiently informative and broadly applicable. We therefore formulate deep research as a query-conditioned report optimization problem with an evaluation bottleneck. In particular, the central challenge in training deep research models is how to evaluate long-form reports in a query-specific and stable manner under limited supervision. 3.2 Overview of SCORE To address this challenge, we propose SCORE, a retrieval-grounded and externally guided evaluator-solver framework for deep research report generation as shown in Figure 2 .
